claims.claim: Protestant Bibles have 66 books, Catholic 73, Orthodox more; chapter divisions 13th century (Stephen Langton), verse numbers 16th (Estienne, 1551).
claims.source: John Barton, A History of the Bible (2019)

claims.claim: Psalm 119 is a 176-verse acrostic of 22 eight-verse sections; vv. 97–104 are the mem section; most scholars date it after the exile.
claims.source: Standard commentaries (e.g. L. C. Allen, Psalms 101–150, WBC)

claims.claim: Hebrew siach (Ps 119:97) means musing/talking over; hagah (Josh 1:8) is used of a dove moaning (Isa 38:14) and a lion growling (Isa 31:4).
Jews say the Shema morning and evening; the mezuzah holds Deut 6:4–9 and 11:13–21.
The KJV was made by about fifty scholars in six companies (Westminster, Oxford, Cambridge), 1604–1611; the preface was written by Miles Smith, later Bishop of Gloucester.
claims.source: David Norton, The King James Bible: A Short History (2011)

claims.claim: The Constitutions of Oxford (drafted 1407, issued 1409) forbade unauthorised English translations.
Acts 15:21 (Moses read every Sabbath); Luke 4:16 (Jesus reads Isaiah at Nazareth).
Justin Martyr, First Apology 67 (c. 155): memoirs of the apostles or writings of the prophets read 'as long as time permits', then a sermon.
Cranmer's 1549 BCP: OT read once a year, NT three times (Revelation excepted), Psalter monthly.
claims.source: BCP 1549 preface 'Concerning the Service of the Church'

claims.claim: M'Cheyne's calendar (Dundee, 1842): four chapters a day, OT once and NT and Psalms twice a year.
claims.source: R. M. M'Cheyne, Calendar for Daily Readings (1842)

claims.claim: Eugene Nida popularised 'dynamic equivalence' (Toward a Science of Translating, 1964).
Translation dates: KJV 1611; NRSV 1989 (NRSVue 2021); ESV 2001; NIV 1978 (2011); NABRE 2011; Orthodox Study Bible 2008.
Jerome translated the Vulgate (c. 382–405); Wycliffite Bible 1380s; Tyndale's NT 1526; Tyndale executed at Vilvoorde near Brussels 1536; Douay–Rheims 1582–1610.
Dei Verbum 22: 'Easy access to Sacred Scripture should be provided for all the Christian faithful.' DV 24 'soul of sacred theology'; DV 25 urges reading.
Augustine 354–430; baptised/converted 386 Milan; bishop of Hippo 395/396; On Christian Doctrine I–III.25 begun 396/397, completed 426–427.
claims.source: Augustine, Retractations II.4; Peter Brown, Augustine of Hippo

claims.claim: Aquinas wrote the Summa Theologiae c. 1265–1273; ST I.1.10 on the senses of Scripture.
Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 63a: 'a verse does not depart from its plain meaning'.
Luther: the Holy Spirit is 'the simplest writer' (Answer to Emser, 1521); OT as swaddling cloths of Christ (Preface to the OT, 1523). Our own words.
Benjamin Jowett, 'On the Interpretation of Scripture', Essays and Reviews (1860): 'Interpret the Scripture like any other book.'
Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943); Pontifical Biblical Commission (1993) calls the historical-critical method 'indispensable'.
claims.source: PBC, The Interpretation of the Bible in the Church (1993), I.A

claims.claim: Antiochene school: Diodore (d. c. 390), Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428, condemned 553), John Chrysostom (c. 347–407).
Augustine, Literal Meaning of Genesis I.19.39, on Christians talking nonsense about nature.
claims.source: Augustine, De Genesi ad litteram I.19.39

claims.claim: Rashi (1040–1105) aimed at the plain meaning; Rashbam (his grandson); Nicholas of Lyra drew on Rashi; Luther used Lyra.
Origen c. 185–253; Hexapla; On First Principles c. 220–230; Book IV in Greek preserved in the Philocalia (Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, c. 360); Rufinus's Latin 398; some teachings condemned 553.
Cassian, Conferences XIV.8: Jerusalem as city, Church, soul, heavenly city.
The couplet 'Littera gesta docet...' is attributed to Augustine of Dacia, Rotulus pugillaris (c. 1260); our translation.
Letter to Can Grande (Epistle XIII, §7) reads Psalm 114 on four levels; authorship debated.
1 Clement 12 reads Rahab's scarlet cord as the blood of Christ; Origen reads the six water jars of Cana (in De Principiis IV.1.12, part omitted from our extract).
Hugh of St Victor: history as the foundation (Didascalicon VI.3).
claims.source: Hugh of St Victor, Didascalicon VI.3

claims.claim: PaRDeS (peshat, remez, derash, sod) appears in 13th-century Jewish mysticism (Moses de León's circle).
Calvin: the true meaning of Scripture is the natural and obvious meaning (Commentary on Galatians 4:22).
Catechism of the Catholic Church 115–119 teaches the four senses.
Henri de Lubac (1896–1991), Medieval Exegesis (1959–64).
Baldung trained/worked in Dürer's workshop (c. 1503–07); painting dated c. 1511.
Mishnah compiled c. 200 by Judah the Prince; Talmud c. 500–600; Avot studied on summer Sabbath afternoons.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.8.1 (mosaic of a king rearranged into a dog or fox) and I.10.1 (rule of faith), c. 180.
Vincent of Lérins, Commonitorium 2 (434): 'everywhere, always, by all'.
Trent Session IV (8 April 1546); Dei Verbum 9–10 phrases quoted.
claims.source: Tanner, Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils; Dei Verbum

claims.claim: Westminster Confession I.9 (1646) quoted; Thirty-Nine Articles VI (1571) quoted; Hooker 1594–97.
Luther at Worms, 18 April 1521: 'testimony of the Scriptures or by clear reason'.
Hillel, b. Shabbat 31a: 'What is hateful to you...' (our rendering).
Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, 1999.
Zurbarán's workshop in Seville; Paula and Eustochium learned Hebrew to read with Jerome.
Douglass born c. 1818 Talbot County, Maryland; escaped 1838; Narrative 1845; My Bondage 1855; speech at Rochester 5 July 1852 at the invitation of the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society.
claims.source: David Blight, Frederick Douglass: Prophet of Freedom (2018)

claims.claim: Thomas Auld converted at a Methodist camp meeting (1832); Sabbath school at St Michael's broken up c. 1833; Henny whipped with Luke 12:47 quoted.
claims.source: My Bondage and My Freedom ch. XIV

claims.claim: Nat Turner's revolt 1831, about 55–60 white people killed; states tightened anti-literacy laws afterwards.
claims.source: Patrick Breen, The Land Shall Be Deluged in Blood (2015)

claims.claim: Fugitive Slave Act 1850; Garrison's Liberator first issue 1831 ('I will not equivocate').
Methodist Episcopal Church split 1844 (MEC South 1845); Southern Baptist Convention 1845.
claims.source: Noll (2006); C. C. Goen, Broken Churches, Broken Nation (1985)

claims.claim: Germantown Quaker petition 1688 from the Golden Rule.
Noll's thesis (pro-slavery side strong on individual texts; common-sense literalism; settled by war), in our own words.
claims.source: Mark Noll, The Civil War as a Theological Crisis (2006)

claims.claim: Stanley Fish, Is There a Text in This Class? (1980): interpretive communities.
Hector Avalos (d. 2021), Slavery, Abolitionism, and the Ethics of Biblical Scholarship (2011): Bible supports slavery; abolitionists read against it.
Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 4 on Ecclesiastes (c. 379), condemns slave-owning as buying the image of God.
claims.source: Gregory of Nyssa, Hom. in Eccl. 4

claims.claim: Nostra Aetate 4 (1965) rejects collective Jewish guilt; WARC Ottawa 1982 declared apartheid theology heresy; DRC later repudiated it.
claims.source: Nostra Aetate; WARC (1982); DRC General Synod 1986/1998

claims.claim: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, The Woman's Bible (1895–98).
Origen's Letter to Gregory (c. 235–240) urges 'divine reading' (theia anagnosis).

Guigo II prior of the Grande Chartreuse c. 1174–1180, d. c. 1188; Scala claustralium to Brother Gervase; four rungs; food and grape images; Matthew 5:8 example; Psalm 24 cited; warnings about rungs without each other; contemplation as gift. All in our own words.
claims.source: Guigo II, The Ladder of Monks, tr. Colledge and Walsh (1978)

claims.claim: Carthusians founded by Bruno of Cologne in 1084.
Rule of Benedict 48: two to three hours of reading a day; a book from the library in Lent; reading in silence after the meal so as not to disturb others.
Bernard preached 86 sermons on the Song of Songs, reaching Song 3:1.
claims.source: Bernard, Sermons on the Song of Songs

claims.claim: Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises approved 1548; 'composition of place'.
Luther, A Simple Way to Pray (1535) for Peter Beskendorf: instruction, thanksgiving, confession, prayer.
Mishnah Peah 1:1: the study of Torah is equal to them all.
Benedict XVI, Verbum Domini 87 (2010), describes lectio's steps.
Thomas à Kempis c. 1380–1471, Mount St Agnes near Zwolle; Imitation c. 1418–27; Latin 'humiliter, simpliciter et fideliter'.
James, brother of Jesus, executed AD 62 (Josephus, Ant. XX.200); authorship debated.
Antony c. 251–356; Augustine says the story of Antony helped his conversion (Confessions VIII.6).
claims.source: Athanasius, Life of Antony; Augustine, Conf. VIII.6

claims.claim: Catholic Lectionary for Mass 1969 (2nd ed. 1981).
Bruckner's Locus iste 1869; Byrd's Mass for Four Voices c. 1592; Missa Papae Marcelli published 1567; Duruflé's Ubi caritas 1960; Allegri's Miserere 1630s; Bach's Jesu, Joy 1723.

Reused paintings: zurbaran-jerome-paula (session 4; also in can-i-trust-the-bible) and bellini-jerome (session 6; can-i-trust-the-bible's journey art). Reused because they show the subject exactly (Scripture read in company; a monk reading).

Luther's Preface to the OT (1523) and Answer to Emser (1521): only post-1929 English translations exist, so in our own words.
Mark Noll's, Stanley Fish's and Hector Avalos's views are summarised in our own words; please check the summaries are fair.

Session 4's table of traditions simplifies; please have Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed and Anglican readers check their own rows, and a Jewish reader the Jewish material (oral Torah, Avot, chavruta, PaRDeS, Rashi).
The Dante letter's authorship is debated; the text says so.
Guigo II is described entirely in our own words; please check the images and the account of his Matthew 5:8 example against Colledge and Walsh's translation.

Guigo II, The Ladder of Monks: no English translation before 1929. In our own words (session 6 lecture). Session 6 reads Thomas à Kempis, Imitation I.5 (Benham) and Rule of Benedict 48 (Henderson), with Luke 10:38–42 as the compare.
Benedict's Rule, Gutenberg #50040, is Doyle (1948), which fails the rule: not used. Henderson (1910, Fordham Sourcebook) is used instead. Gasquet was not found.
Luther, Preface to the Old Testament: only the 1932 Jacobs translation. Session 2's compare is Aquinas ST I.1.10, reply to objection 3, and Luther is in our own words.
Pirkei Avot: the cached file is Oesterley (1919), not Charles Taylor as the plan said. Oesterley (d. 1950) qualifies, so he is used.
Augustine of Dacia's couplet: Latin quoted, our own translation.
Galatians 4:21–31 is read in Abraham and the promise, so it is pointed back to and not re-read. Psalm 1, Nehemiah 8, Luke 24 and Acts 8 are pointed back to, as the spec asks.
